speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture. subtopic: REASON FOR REDUCTION IN SUBSIDY

In connection with the question of the hon. member, there is a long and complicated story as to how the stabilization board operates so far as cheese is concerned, but the answer to the question is that there was a subsidy of 4 cents a pound on cheese which was recommended by the stabilization board. The stabilization board felt there should be a reduction of 1 cent because it was not required any longer with Canadian Cheddar cheese, which was selling at a premium in Great Britain; so they recommended that the 1 cent be taken off.
I can assure the hon. member that Canadian cheese in Great Britain is selling at a premium, and there is a big difference between New Zealand cheese and Canadian cheese. He might also be interested to know that the price of milk used in the manufacture of cheese is now higher than it has been for a number of years. I think the producers are quite happy about this, and there is still a big demand for Canadian Cheddar cheese.
With regard to the second question, I can assure the hon. member that the cheese board have no intention of putting anyone out of business. All they are interested in is selling as much Canadian cheese as possible, and this is being done. We could sell more cheese than we are manufacturing, and we are trying to convert from butter to cheese. In this regard we had a big disappearance of butter from the market last May and a larger one in June.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of
Trade and Commerce. As of noon today I was informed by his department that there were still 29 points on a 10 bushel quota.

Since there is only one day of the old crop year remaining, how does he expect to meet his goal of 12 bushels, and how does he expect the farmers to deliver the two bushels in the one remaining day if there are no box cars?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORTED INABILITY TO DELIVER QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre asked a similar question and 1 promised I would have a statement early this week. I should like to make that statement now in reply to this question. I regret that the statement is rather lengthy, but I feel the subject is probably important enough to warrant it.
The Canadian wheat board has advised me that as at noon today there were 1,891 delivery points in western Canada on a quota of 12 bushels per specified acre out of a total of 1,942. Of the remaining 51 points, 22 of these have been closed and 29, as the hon. member for Mackenzie said, are still on a quota of 10 bushels per specified acre. Of those points on a 10 bushel quota, 25 are located in the province of Saskatchewan and 4 in the province of Alberta. Despite the concentration of shipments between now and the end of the crop year, some of these 29 stations will still be on a 10 bushel quota at the end of the crop year on July 31.
Early in June the board forwarded special questionnaire No. 3 to all delivery points requesting agents to estimate the quantity of all grains deliverable by producers in the 1962-63 crop year. The information received by the board from the agents as a result of this questionnaire showed the following estimates as at June 7, 1963:
Millions of Bushels
Wheat	430.8
Durum	59.3
Oats	95.1
Barley	77.0
Rye	9.6
Flax	13.7
Total	685.5
Producers' marketings to June 7 totalled 475.4 million bushels, leaving a total of 210.1 million bushels to be delivered between June 7 and July 31 to take all grain off farms. After considering the disappearance in export and domestic markets during the period June 7 to July 31, 1963, it was apparent to the board that it would be impossible to provide space for the delivery of 210.1 million bushels of grain within the period June 7 to July 31. However, in order to permit producers deliveries to the maximum possible, the board decided to set as a target a quota of 12 bushels per specified acre for all delivery points by July 31, 1963, which would
Inquiries of the Ministry involve the delivery of about 153.1 million bushels, thus leaving approximately 57 million bushels on farms at the end of the crop year.
The necessary shipping orders were placed to meet this target and the railways were requested to exert every effort to supply box cars in order that the goal of 12 bushels per specified acre could be attained. The Canadian wheat board states that the cooperation received from the railways has been excellent and the railways are continuing to supply box cars to the maximum extent possible.
However, in an operation of this magnitude it is inevitable that difficulties will arise which will adversely affect some areas. While, in the opinion of the board, these difficulties have not been major, nevertheless they have had the effect of hampering the attainment of the target quota. The latest records available to the board indicate that as of July 24 the estimated quantity still to be delivered to complete a 12 bushel quota was approximately 29 million bushels. The railway companies are maintaining shipments at maximum, and a considerable portion of this 29 million bushels will be delivered to country elevators by the end of the crop year.
In summary, the majority of the shipping points in western Canada will, by July 31, have marketed a full 12 bushel quota. Some points, while on a 12 bushel quota, will not have the opportunity to deliver all the grain represented by that quota, but they will have had the opportunity of delivering all grain represented by an 11 bushel quota. As previously stated, a minimum number of stations will still be on a 10 bushel quota.
The target of 12 bushels per specified acre was based on the information contained in special questionnaire No. 3, to which I have already referred; but since the results of this questionnaire were received a great many points have advised that additional quantities have been revealed which were not reported to the board in the questionnaire.
The board has taken the stand that it cannot give effect to these additional quantities of grain in its computations, as to do so would completely disrupt the plans that were laid with the railway companies to provide box cars on the basis of information previously received as at June 7. There is no doubt this situation has developed because of the excellent crop conditions now prevailing, and producers therefore have decided to deliver stocks which they had been holding in reserve.
The board also advises that instructions in regard to quotas have been issued to the trade that the present crop year will end at

Inquiries of the Ministry midnight on July 31. The board is not prepared to extend the year end date, as previous experience in this regard has shown that any such action unduly delays the delivery of the unit quota in the new crop year.
The board regrets that this action will doubtless adversely affect, to some degree, a limited number of producers, but in the main this decision will be in the best interests of producers as a whole.

I am very pleased, particularly in view of what I thought was an uncalled for reflection by the hon. member for Port Arthur, to which I took no exception, to have an opportunity to put the record straight in connection with this matter.
I might start by saying that the board of broadcast governors has not yet given approval to this matter, and therefore it is not yet within the power of the government to take any action with regard to it. The fact is that certain conditions were attached to this recommendation of the board of broadcast governors on April 5. I could give the house these conditions, but I do not want to go into all that detail. Then on April 17, five days before the present government came into office, the board received a letter from the deputy minister of transport asking to have a clarification of those conditions before a recommendation was made to the Minister of Transport. I am not suggesting this was done by any minister; all I am pointing out is that it was done before the present government came Lu office. I jusi want io make the date clear. The chairman of the board replied on April 13 to this effect:
I shall, as soon as possible, write you further on the other conditions which the board recommended by application in the case of the St. John's station.
I consulted the chairman of the board of broadcast governors this morning and he informed me that on June 28 he wrote to the vice president, corporative affairs, C.B.C., as follows in reply to a letter received from the corporation:
We are reluctant at this time to spell out more precisely the general conditions attached to the board's recommendations in this case. The expansion of C.B.C. facilities with consequent disaffiliation of private stations is among the matters being discussed by Mr. Ouimet, Mr. Jamieson and myself at the request of the minister (the Secretary of State) and with a view to reporting to the minister. The procedures involved in expansion of the C.B.C. facilities including alternative network service to the disaffiliated stations the availability and economical use of microwave facilities, the relation of assisting rebroadcasting stations to the extension of alternative service, etc. are important. While individual cases may differ in some respects it seems desirable to establish some principles applicable to all cases of the expansion of second service into smaller centres, including St. John's. Agreement on these principles should, we believe, precede a more precise definition of the conditions applicable to the St. John's case and, therefore, we feel we are not in a position to meet the request of the Minister of Transport at this time.
Now, until the board has made that recommendation the government has no legal authority to act.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I am not in a position at this time to give a satisfactory answer as to the immediate possibility of a settlement of the British Columbia fishing strike. However, with the permission of the house may I read a press release that is being issued at this very moment. It is a joint press release issued by the federal government and the government of British Columbia, and reads as follows:
The federal Minister of Fisheries and the minister of labour for British Columbia met all day
Inquiries of the Ministry
yesterday in Vancouver to consider the present crisis in the British Columbia fishing industry. The current dispute is primarily concerned with the minimum prices to be received by fishermen from the sale of fish and no effective procedures presently exist to resolve this problem. In considering the current serious situation it was agreed that the fishermen should be urged to return to work forthwith. While there may be a valid dispute between the union and the fisheries association, it does however prevent the harvesting of this valuable resource. Unless fishing is resumed immediately some runs will be missed completely and some may be damaged by excessive spawning escapement.
The fishery resource is one whose harvest must be kept under strict control. Failure to harvest, with overseeding of spawning beds, could be as disastrous as overtake. A balance has to be maintained to keep stocks at a high productive level.
It is the joint recommendation of both governments that fishing be resumed immediately and that the matters in dispute be submitted to arbitration for final and binding decision. To expedite the proceedings the federal and provincial governments are prepared to appoint on request, if the parties agree, a single arbitrator to commence hearings immediately.
However, no further losses to the workmen, the industry or the national economy should be allowed to continue and hence the recommendation that fishing be resumed forthwith. To seek a long term solution to the problem the federal and provincial governments have agreed to appoint a committee consisting of three representatives of the federal government and three representatives of the provincial government to examine in detail the problems concerned with price and wage disputes in the British Columbia fishing industry and to submit to both governments recommendations of action necessary to minimize interruptions of fishing operations in the future.

The house resumed, from Thursday, July 25, consideration in committee of Bill No. [Mr. BalcerJ
C-90, to amend the Excise Tax Act-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 4-Refund of tax paid on goods for use in sewerage or drainage systems.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
During the consideration of clause 4 of the bill last Thursday evening there was considerable discussion concerning the fact that certain areas are not called municipalities, and a number of hon. members offered suggestions about what should or should not be classed as municipalities. I promised to look into the matter, and I have had an opportunity of doing so in the meantime. I have been able to examine carefully the various suggestions put forward by hon. members, and I now have an amendment which the Secretary of State wishes to place before the committee to define the scope of the term "municipality".
When we began to examine this matter, even before Thursday, we found it to be more complicated than at first it appeared. On Thursday evening several members, including the hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Royal, suggested that anything which a province declared to be or designated as a municipality should also be classed as a municipality for the purposes of the Excise Tax Act. We found, however, that the provinces sometimes defined municipalities in different ways for different purposes in different acts. There would have been some uncertainty as to which definition would apply. Moreover, there is no uniformity among provinces in the way in which they define municipalities. Therefore to accept a provincial definition might have given more generous exemption in one province than in another.
Now, in searching for a definition we had to keep in mind that there must be some government body to which the exemptions could be extended or refunds paid. The exemption from sales tax for certain municipal purchases is not a direct exemption for individuals, although of course individuals residing in the municipalities benefit. This is an exemption for a governing body to help it meet the serious problem of financing the expansion of public services in its area.
Subject to this requirement, it was our aim to make the definition as broad as possible. We are therefore proposing a definition of municipality which will be very similar to the definition which it is proposed to use in the municipal development and loan act. The definition proposed refers to city, town, village, district, rural municipality or other incorporated municipal body; that is, it refers specifically to all the forms of organization

generally regarded as providing local government. However, because of the difficulty of foreseeing or describing other kinds of local authorities which may develop from time to time, it is proposed, if this is agreeable to hon. members of the committee, that the definition contain a provision giving the governor in council power to determine that such other local authority as the governor in council may determine, shall be a municipality for the purpose of this act.
It is a question whether the members of the committee wish to give this power to the governor in council. Short of that it will be very difficult to arrive at a definition that will cover every conceivable set of circumstances. I think it should be noted that the definition proposed will apply to the important list of exemptions for municipal purchases already in the Excise Tax Act as well as exemption for materials for sewerage and drainage systems described in the bill now before the committee. For that reason it is suggested that the clauses be renumbered so that this definition will appear at the beginning of the bill. The words which appear at the end of clause 4 read as follows:
For the purpose of this subsection any agency operating a sewerage or drainage system for or on behalf of a municipality may be declared by the minister to be a municipality.
These words were added to the act in 1958, when the exemptions for materials purchased by municipalities for sewerage and drainage systems were included. The purpose of these words is to extend the exemption to agencies such as the Ontario water resources commission, and it is proposed to retain these words in the existing clause 4.
Will the minister agree this presupposes the existence of a municipality?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.
And if you have not got the initial municipality you cannot have an agency.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the hon. member for Edmonton West has pointed out, this is the problem and it is a very difficult one. There must be some agency of some incorporated body to whom the refunds can be made. It is not intended to make these refunds payable to individuals, and this I think will cover the points that were raised on Thursday.

Could the minister say
whether in his opinion this new amendment would apply to the provincial bodies I mentioned, such as local government districts? These areas are eligible under the winter works program. They are not municipalities in the correct sense of the word, but they
Excise Tax Act
are eligible under the winter works program, and I would hope they would be included in this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before we talk about it I wonder if we could have the amendment read. I think it will be a little easier then; but to answer the question quickly, it will be possible under the proposed amendment for the Minister of National Revenue to recommend that this be done by order in council. It will be the intention to cover the kind of municipalities which the hon. member has in mind. I do not know any other way of bringing them in under the net except by doing this.
Before I ask the Secretary of State to move this amendment concerning municipalities I should also like to say that I have reviewed the representations made by hon. members, especially by the hon. member for York-Humber and the hon. member for Port Arthur, and by the others outside the house, to the effect that the exception for building materials for schools and universities should be extended to cover building materials for use in the construction of public libraries. We have come to the conclusion that such an exemption should be provided, and when the amendment concerning municipalities has been dealt with and we move on to clause 5 we shall put forward an amendment to that effect.

Sometimes under the law a person is forced by the health act of a province or municipality to put in a sewerage system, and I would ask the minister whether some clause could be introduced to give the same treatment to an individual as to a municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would open the matter up further than I think the government would be prepared to go. There are all sorts of restrictions and rules imposed, not only by the municipalities, but by the provincial governments. For example, there are building regulations which require individuals to build certain types of houses, and it would not be the intention in that case to relieve them of paying this particular tax. The great trouble about this as I think we all appreciate by now, is the question of knowing where to draw the line. In this case it was thought we would be in difficulty if we went further than the amendment which the Secretary of State was on the point of moving a few moments ago.

I know of a case where a man is being forced to do this work. If he comes within the two years he is all right, but if it is over that he is caught and the municipality will be taking over the area and incorporating it. This is going to be very unfair on an individual who is living on the outskirts of a municipality. If a provincial or

Excise Tax Act
municipal board of health forces a person to do this then, with all due respect to the minister, I feel we should give the individual a break.

I would like to ask the
minister how much revenue is involved in this obviously complicated clause. If it is not such a huge amount perhaps he might consider other points, and might even consider withdrawing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a substantial amount. I do not think anybody can tell exactly, but if we start to make exemptions for people living in rural areas there will be quite a conflict with people living in urban areas, and the hope is that they will be treated on substantially the same basis. That is why if we start making exemptions for individuals, we will be in real trouble unless we make them for all individuals, and if we make them for all individuals then there is no point in distinguishing whether the work is for a drainage or sewerage system. You might as well apply the exemption to all building materials, and the first thing we will know is that we have not got a tax at all.
Could the minister indicate any round figure of revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is any way of giving an estimate that I would be happy about. It depends on how far the exemption suggested by the hon. member for Simcoe East would go. I do not think you can limit it to people in rural municipalities.

This is an unusual situation. The minister proposes to introduce a tax and he has no idea how much revenue will be brought in by it. If he has no idea then maybe it will not bring in anything. On the other hand it may bring in $100 million. If it were something like $500,000 then it might be unnecessary because it would cost a lot of money to collect it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have some estimate of the totals involved. At 4 per cent the totals involved come to something over $100 million for all the things that will be covered. One would have to be very precise in knowing what the additional exemption might involve before any kind of estimate could be made about that, but the more exemptions are made the more difficulties are encountered.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this session I asked the Minister of Finance a question similar to the one I am going to ask now. The minister referred the matter to the Minister of National Revenue at that time. I do not see it mentioned in the bill
that is before us, so I would like to get some confirmation on whether consideration has been given to municipalities which have committed themselves, not by tender but by bylaw, to putting up public buildings such as city halls, where the actual contract has not been submitted. They will now be caught between a fixed price under the by-law and a contract price that has been called. I asked at the time whether it would be possible under circumstances of this type to have it considered as a contract. It is definitely a contract between the municipal and city authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether the hon. member would be willing to wait until we get to the clause of the bill dealing with refunds generally. I think it is clause 9.
Perhaps before this particular amendment is moved I might also refer to the question of certain building materials that are competitive. We have tried to take into account those situations where the imposition of the sales tax on building materials may result in serious competitive inequality where goods fabricated off the site of construction compete directly with goods that can be constructed on the site. In line with this purpose the bill contains a provision to provide that prefabricated buildings will not be taxable on their selling price, and the manufacturers of such buildings will have to pay sales tax on the materials they purchase. Similarly the manufacturers of structural building sections such as precast, prestressed concrete building sections or pillars are not regarded as manufacturers for sales tax purposes because these products compete with concrete sections that can be poured as the building is erected. The same rule will apply for manufacturers of concrete or cinder building blocks because these compete with poured concrete walls.
It has now been brought to our attention that a similar situation exists with respect to structural steel for buildings, which of course competes directly with prestressed forms. It is usual for the steel that goes into a building to be designed and cut to size on the premises of fabricating companies and delivered to the building site ready for erection. This steel competes directly with reinforced concrete poured on the site. In the case of concrete poured on site the labour involved does not enter into the base for sales tax. In the case of steel the labour involved in fabricating does become part of the price that is subject to sales tax. It is therefore proposed that an amendment be made which will have the effect of excluding from the base for sales tax that part of the selling price of steel which arises from the fabricating work done off the

building site. It will take the form of a further paragraph to the new subclause (2b) added by clause 2 on page 1. The effect of this amendment will be that fabricators of structural steel for buildings will buy steel on which the sales tax is imposed but will not have to pay sales tax on the fabricated structural steel they sell.

There is one other area, Mr. Chairman, where I think there is an unfair competitive advantage. This matter has been brought to my attention since we passed clause 2, and I am very happy that the minister has mentioned it. I refer to the unwarranted competitive advantage given to what may be interpreted as building bricks or concrete bricks and cinder blocks. Over the past few years-I think it is fairly recent- the concrete block industry have developed a product that is very, very similar to the burnt brick in colour, size, etc. In the case of burnt brick the manufacturers are required to pay sales tax, I understand, under the bill that is being considered, on the clay, firing, labour and all the other component costs that go into the finished product; whereas with a concrete brick or block they are exempt from sales tax, I take it, in relation to the labour and the aggregate, which is the block, of course. The only thing they would pay sales tax on would be the cement that went into the concrete block.
I know there are going to be problems in making a ruling and an interpretation that would not change the competitive factor between these two types of bricks. But I would like to point out to the minister that there is very definitely, I think, an unwarranted competitive advantage given to the manufacturers of this type of brick in relation to the situation that existed previously. I wonder whether the minister would care to comment on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member has very successfully pointed out- more successfully than perhaps I have- the difficulty of knowing where to draw the line in these things. If you extend this to ordinary bricks that are fired or burnt in a kiln, then I presume the next question would be, should you not exclude lumber or steel siding or any of the other building materials that can be used as alternatives. The Minister of Finance has reminded me that the amendment, with which I am not very familiar, not yet having read it, will be to insert a new paragraph 1 which will provide a definition of "municipality". This might abbreviate some of the other discussion, and if the committee would like me to move it now I shall be very glad to do so. I will read it slowly so that everyone will be able to absorb it, including the mover. I move:
That Bill C-90, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act, be amended by renumbering clauses 1 to 9 thereof as clauses 2 to 10 respectively and by adding thereto as clause 1 thereof the following:

1. Subsection (1) of section 2 of the Excise Tax Act is amended by adding thereto, immediately after paragraph (b) thereof, the following paragraph :
"Municipality".
"(ba) "municipality" means (i) an incorporated city, metropolitan authority, town, village, township, district or rural municipality or other incorporated municipal body however designated, or
(ii) such other incorporated local authority as the governor in council may determine to be a municipality for the purposes of this act;"

In connection with that amendment, may I ask how it is that the federal government can define what is a municipality? I think it is the responsibility of the provincial authorities to determine what is a municipality. Here a decision is, apparently, to be made by order in council, and there is no reference to provincial jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member could not have been here when I was explaining this.
I was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then he will remember that I said the difficulty about relying entirely on the provinces in this matter is that they have defined municipalities in different ways in different acts; it is a question of which provincial definitions could be used. Apart from this there is considerable difference between the definitions used by some provinces and those used by others. The definition proposed here includes all incorporated bodies which could conceivably be called municipalities now, but it does leave some leeway in case some situation develops where there is in fairness an obvious need for exemption to put some new body on the same terms as existing ones.
As I said earlier, if members of the committee are prepared to accept this proposal we would be glad to see it go through; but if hon. members do not like it, this part would have to be dropped.
Can the minister assure that under this definition no municipalities considered as such by any province in Canada will be left out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly can give that assurance.

The minister is attempting in this amendment to clarify the definition of certain words. I think they are not the only phrases to need clarification. When this bill is passed by this house in its final form it becomes law under the title, "An act to amend the Excise Act". It is obvious, if we recall the debates and the remarks made by the minister, that there are parts of the bill we do not understand, in particular the 28902-5-178
Excise Tax Act
definitions of certain words or terms. If this measure is passed without amendment or explanation the confusion which will exist when the public and the officials of the department begin dealing with these terms can readily be imagined. How can we, as members of parliament, expect the public and the officials to understand the act if we do not understand it ourselves?
The minister could prevent much of this confusion if he would insert a short clause to the effect that in the absence of definition in the Excise Tax Act, the definition of any term will be that found in an accepted dictionary. If such a proposal as this is not included we might as well scrap the entire wording of this bill and insert just two lines to read "The act is amended as interpreted by the official dealing with the subject matter contained in the act". I make this comment because, in reality, this is what we are doing; we are passing the buck.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member-

I am not yet finished. I would say that by our actions we are making a bureaucratic dictatorship out of our civil servants. The fault does not lie with the civil servants, but with the past and present members of this house. Too often in the past, as is evidenced by the contents of other acts, we have transferred our responsibilities as representatives of the people of Canada over to the bureaucrats. One of the results of our irresponsible actions is that the public takes its problems or cases to the tariff board or to the courts of the land, a costly procedure to the federal treasury as well as to individuals trapped by careless legislation. I am informed that under certain sections of this act, sections which parliament has passed, the public is not given the right to appeal to the courts but must, by law, accept the decisions of the officials.
I am sure many of the officials themselves do not relish the task of having to make decisions relating to so many of these undefined terms in the act. They feel, and rightly so, that this is the responsibility of parliament. This was referred to in a letter I received from an Ontario citizen which reads in part:
Naturally, I felt that at least our government should be as fair as companies doing business. I went to Ottawa and had an interview with Mr	 but he put all the blame on the members
who had approved the paragraph in the tax bill.
And rightly so. There are a number of terms contained in clause 6 which, if not defined, will lead to a great deal of misunderstanding between the public and the officials of the department. Some of these misunderstandings, I have no doubt, will result in costly court cases. I refer to such

Excise Tax Act
words as "wagon" and "manufacturers". I know one citizen from my constituency who spent an amount in excess of $500 endeavouring unsuccessfully to get a ruling from the department on the meaning of the term "wagon". Because the department will neither accept any legal interpretation nor provide a definition which they will accept, all farmers purchasing steel grain truck boxes must pay an additional $300 to $400 on such a purchase.
On page 694, volume 1, 1952, Revised Statutes of Canada, under the Canadian Grain Act, "wagon" is defined as any vehicle used to deliver grain to the country elevators. The Department of National Revenue will not accept the definition of the word "wagon" contained in the Excise Tax Act, nor any dictionary definition.
Members of the minister's own profession are greatly concerned about the misunderstandings caused by the lack of definition of terms used in this act. I refer the hon. gentleman to an article which appeared in the publication entitled "The Canadian Chartered Accountant", volume 2, No. 5, dated May, 1953. The heading is "Sales Tax-Who is a Manufacturer?" I should like to read part of this article. It says:
The most important taxing provision in the Excise Tax Act, section 30(1) (a), imposes a consumption or sales tax on the sale price of all goods ''produced or manufactured in Canada". Since this tax is payable by the "producer or manufacturer", it frequently becomes important to know whether a particular person is a manufacturer for sales tax purposes or whether he is merely a distributor, jobber, retailer or consumer, none of whom are liable to pay sales tax under section 30(1) (a).
In this article, the term "manufacturer" should be understood to refer to a "producer or manufacturer" for the purposes of the Excise Tax Act.
The statutory provisions, regulations and rulings dealing with this question are unusually complex. Although the Excise Tax Act contains no general definitions of the expressions "produced or manufactured" or "producer or manufacturer", there are a number of provisions in the act and in the regulations and rulings made under its authority stating that such diverse activities as packaging candies, setting diamonds in rings, repairing fur garments and printing stationery are to be treated as manufacturing operations for sales tax purposes, but that making popcorn, cider or false teeth or developing and printing photographs are not to be so treated. In addition, there are a considerable number of decided cases in which the courts have been asked to rule on such activities-
I could go on and inform the minister of what his colleagues have said about this act but I think I should say the sales tax should be imposed upon persons who manufacture foods and not upon one who merely provides a service. The difference between a contract for the sale of goods and a contract for services or for labour and materials is well known in common law but apparently

not by the Department of National Revenue. Once you are designated by the department as a manufacturer, whether you are or not you are compelled to take out a manufacturer's licence. You are then subject to further rules and regulations compiled by the officials of the department. I refer now to such regulations as regulation 2 contained in circular ET.l, which is all-powerful' and generally not known to the public but only to the retailer, jobber or distributor who is compelled to enforce the provisions of the regulations.
Under these regulations, with special formula compiled by the officials, the retailer is forced to impose an additional hidden tax on the consumer, an additional 4 per cent sales tax calculated on the cost of the article plus the added amount of 11 per cent sales tax already included in the cost price. Possibly the reluctance to define these terms is for a purpose. Because they are not defined the department has made use of this method to collect many thousands of dollars for the federal treasury. Although I agree the treasury needs the money, this is no manner in which to collect needed revenue. I would urge the minister to specify in the bill as I have suggested a source of interpretation acceptable to his department as well as to the Department of National Revenue.
I have some things I want to say on clause 6 when it comes up in regard to some of the terms that are used there, but at this time I would ask the minister if he would accept the suggestion I have put forward.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not a member of the legal profession, and I think that is something I may share in common with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. I am informed by members of the legal profession that the suggestion made by the hon. member, to which I must say I listened with great interest, would not be entirely satisfactory. I am sure we would not be able to recommend an amendment here that had not been approved by the Department of Justice. That is the difficulty.
I think that some of the points the hon. member made are very pertinent and understandable, but I am afraid that if we embarked upon a complete revision of the Excise Tax Act at this particular stage we would find that a great deal of preparatory work was needed before this committee could usefully deal with that kind of task.

I am very surprised the minister says that the legal department does not consider this possible because the very article from which I quoted states that when

these cases are taken to the courts the judges look first to the ordinary dictionary definitions to make their rulings. If the federal treasury is going to be put to the additional cost of taking cases to court and the public also are going to be put to the cost of taking cases to court only to have judges resort to dictionaries to define the meaning of certain words, why can we not put it in the act in the first place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I have not been here long enough. I do not know who passed the act in the first place, but in dealing with amendments to the act I do not think we should include a wide variety of definitions that might upset a series of legal precedents on this very point that the hon. member has raised.
I will not argue about the rest of the act, but will the minister do it for the part contained in this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that if we tried to include definitions in the bill that applied only to certain sections or subsections of the act we would be in a great deal of difficulty.
Would the minister not agree with me that if these terms cannot be defined there is no use putting them in the bill? We do not know what they mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think all I can say is that many of these words have been interpreted in the courts over a long period, but I am not a lawyer and I cannot answer the question more specifically than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: So that there will be no misunderstanding at all, the hon. member will see that the second section applies to "such other incorporated local authority". It does not include a wide area that has no status as such under provincial law. The reason for that, as I have said before, is that if the provinces concerned do not look upon the area as some official kind of area which they are prepared to incorporate it will not qualify under this provision.

I wish to say a few words on that point. I think the whole matter could be clarified if certain words were deleted from subsection 2 of this amendment. An incorporated municipality is one that has been given permission by a municipal board to incorporate itself. But an unorganized territory is one that is under the direct supervision of a municipal board where a trusteeship is set up to look after the area. An example of that is Elliot Lake and other areas of that kind. They are directly responsible to the municipal board. They are not responsible to the electors of the district at all. If the words "incorporated local" were deleted the section would then read:
(ii) such other authority as the governor in council may determine to be a municipality for the purposes of this act.
In most cases the province acts on behalf of these areas. The province calls for tenders for any construction work that is to be done or any improvements that are to be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I answer both hon. members. If the province is acting for these areas, then I think they are exempt because provinces are exempt. Certainly, therefore, the type of area to which the hon. member for Ontario referred, which I think he said would be administered by the province, would be exempt because the province would be doing the buying. I think probably the same answer applies in your case, too.

This is a question of the minister relating back to the explanation he has just given. I hope the exemption is not limited to the province doing the buying on behalf of some of these communities because in British Columbia there are communities, not organized territories, not incorporated communities, but unorganized territories in which the taxes are collected by the province and such administration as there is is the responsibility of the provincial department of municipal affairs. Excise Tax Act
so on. Under the winter works program, a number of these communities in British Columbia were able to participate on the recommendation of the department of municipal affairs. I assume the same condition would apply under this definition?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would be glad to consider that, Mr. Chairman, and discuss it with my colleagues. covers water improvement districts, fire improvement districts and so on in British Columbia which I believe are actually incorporated under our British Columbia water act. (b) any organization for use exclusively in the construction of a building for that organization that is to be used exclusively or mainly as a public library operated by or on behalf of that organization on a non-commercial basis, and the tax imposed by Part VI has been paid in respect of those materials, the minister, may, upon application of such institution or organization in such form as the minister prescribes made to the minister within two years from the time the materials were purchased, pay to such institution or organization an amount equal to that tax.

On July 8, regarding the schools and universities, the minister indicated that construction materials for such projects could be exempted, as in the case of hospitals which have a 100 per cent exemption. However I feel that the tax means that schools and universities will be paying 11 per cent on such major items as electric fixtures, freight and capacity elevators and air shafts, hot water heaters, floors, air conditioners, pipes, valves and fittings, sprinkler systems, cupboard doors, hinges, nails and other fasteners. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

So, in effect the impression given by the minister that schools and universities would be exempted in the same way as hospitals is not true, because whereas hospitals have a 100 per cent exemption, these have not. I think there is confusion created in the minds of people with regard to this particular aspect.

I have had several representations from steel fabricating people in regard to reinforced structural flooring, roof decks, wall panels and so on. Would this amendment exempt any of those materials used in these buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I would like to suggest that the minister change a few words in this clause and amendment. For instance, the terminology used states:
The minister may, upon application of such institution or organization in such form as the minister prescribes-
By using the word "may", the minister is not obliged to do this, and I ask why not use the word "must".
Further on it says:
-pay to such institution or organization an amount equal to that tax.

Why not use the same expression as used in clause 4, "refund", instead of "an amount equal to that tax"? As it stands now, especially in the French translation, it means that the minister may, if he wishes, give a grant or an exemption to such institutions. I am asking the minister to consider changing those words to mean that in fact an institution will be entitled to a refund of tax which it would have paid on building construction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the advantage of the hon. member for Lapointe because, as he knows, I am not a member of the legal profession; but these particular words to which he has referred are used in other places in the bill, and I think they are inserted in the amendment for that purpose. My hon. friend, the Minister of Forestry, has the advantage of being able to discuss these matters on the same ground as the hon. member for Lapointe.

These words may be used in some other places, but when the question of schools and universities is involved I think the words should be changed. For example we have the words "the minister may" in the English version and in the French version we have tne words "ie minisire peul". I would like the minister, of his own volition, to change the words in this clause and propose an amendment in order to achieve this. Would the minister agree to do that?

If it means "must" in the English version and the French version, I am satisfied.

The verb "peut" means is free to, is not obliged to. So, from the constitutional point of view, it might be preferable in this instance to substitute to the word "peut" in the French text, the words "il doit" as, otherwise, it implies that he is not obliged to do it. (Text) :

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

This is an important matter because it concerns the question of education and our schools and universities. Just while the amendment is being considered I should like to say that I have had experience with representations, and my understanding is that goods used in these buildings must pay tax. I should like to say a few words with regard to clause 6, Mr. Chairman. From reading the supplementary budget speech I understand it was intended to remove the sales tax on materials consumed or expended in a manufacturing process and I believe subclauses 5 and 6 of clause 6 carry out that intent.
I understand that previously machinery and apparatus to be used in manufacture or production were in the same category as there was no object in distinguishing the

two. As a result past decisions by departmental officials have determined that certain things are machinery and not materials used or consumed in production, even though those materials may be consumed within the period of a year. I think there have already been decisions on such items as papermakers' felts. How papermakers' felts could be machines I do not know. In any event, this had to be determined. I am wondering why there could not be a simple definition. Any past definitions are obviously an anachronism because of the new concept that production machinery must be made deductible in order that our manufacturers may be competitive and in particular that they may be able to compete in world markets, which is so necessary.
We certainly do not want to impose a tax on production materials that are consumed by calling those materials machinery and forcing the manufacturer to depreciate them over whatever period of time depreciation may be allowed. I wonder whether we could not implement the distinction already in the Income Tax Act with regard to materials that must be depreciated and which can be called an expense in one year under that act. In other words, if a material is consumed or expended in the taxation year, and normally in one year, then it is a production material consumed in production. If, on the other hand, the item lasts more than one year in the normal course then it is machinery and must be depreciated.
This is the case under the Income Tax Act and I suggest with respect that it would obviate a great deal of difficulty in fighting over every little item to determine what is machinery or materials consumed in the period of one year. I think we would save our industrialists a great deal of concern and possibly a great deal of expense. In my view the departmental officials would have something much simpler to work with if we merely used the same definition as is found in the Income Tax Act. If it is normally consumed in one year it is a production material and is deductible; if, on the other hand, it lasts more than one year it is machinery. I would ask the minister to take that point into consideration and, if it is valid, come up with a definition along those lines, because I think it would simplify the matter a great deal.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. member for Renfrew South because I have a point to bring up with regard to production machinery which is along similar lines. I notice that in clause 6 there is a long list of food products both for man and beast, and a long list of machinery pertaining to the production of foods for man and beast. I also notice that around
Excise Tax Act
line 30 on page 3 there is provision for the exemption of farm produce sold by the individual farmer of his own production. The result is that one of our basic industries is well protected by way of exemption. In line 21 on page 4 there is a reference to sap spouts and sap buckets. My grandfather used to call sap spouts spiles, but that is an almost forgotten word. However, the department correctly lists them descriptively as sap spouts, and refers to other things that are used in connection with our basic maple sugar and syrup industry.
We have another industry that is probably not so productive in dollar value as the maple syrup industry but yet is a very basic industry and one which is vital to some of our agricultural people. In addition, it is found in many parts of Canada such as British Columbia, Ontario and Nova Scotia. I refer to cider production. I notice there is no consideration given here to the cider producers, the farmer or orchardist who produces cider from salvaged windfall apples for his own use and for local sale. I am sure if the minister had ever had a drink of freshly pressed cold sweet cider produced by the farmers of Prince Edward county. Ontario, not Prince Edward Island, he would readily grant a little protection to these people who have to buy the necessary cider presses and tanks in order to make the product.
I simply bring forward this point for the minister's consideration. I should like to see clause 6 amended on page 4 somewhere near the maple syrup item, because the point I am trying to make is that there is an affinity between maple syrup and cider manufacturing. In both cases the producers are usually farmers who are producing a primary product, and I submit that the cider producer deserves as much consideration as the maple syrup producer who has been protected from sales tax for a good many years. I have had two appeals on the part of farmers and orchardists during the past eight months who have strongly protested the fact that they have to pay 11 per cent sales tax on cider press machinery. My amendment to clause 6 would be as follows:
Apple pulp grinders, tanks and presses and complete parts thereof, when used exclusively by farmers and orchardists on their own premises, for the production of apple cider for non-alcoholic use.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister will realize that some of us are not too happy with his excuse that he is not a lawyer when we ask for the interpretation of certain terms. Now that he has his battery of lawyers and consultants in front of him, who I imagine drew up the bill, he should be able to get a legal interpretation of some

Excise Tax Act
of these terms. On page 3, line 24, the phrase "boxes for farm wagons" is used. Would the minister take the definition in the Canada Grain Act for the definition of a wagon? In that act a wagon is defined as meaning "any vehicle used to deliver grain to a country elevator". I should also like to draw the minister's attention to page 4, line 7, where the words "logs and round unmanufactured timber" appear. I wonder whether fence posts, which are small logs sharpened to a point on one end with an axe, are manufactured or not manufactured?
I should like also to draw the minister's attention to line 25, page 4, where a reference is made to forage wagons for off-highway use. I wonder how the department is going to determine whether or not this equipment is for off-highway use. Is there going to be an end user's certificate required, or what procedure will be followed by a person requesting this exemption?
I should like to draw the minister's attention to an item on page 5, line 8, where there is a reference to soft drinks. Line 7 refers to bases or concentrates for making soft drinks, and these are not included. Perhaps The minister has not had any representations from the soft drink manufacturers, but his predecessor had, and it was contended this was a discriminatory tax because they are directly competing with the retailers of tea and coffee. These people asked why their beverages should be taxed while tea and coffee were not taxed. I hope the minister will have an answer in connection with that item.
Then, on page 6, line 20, there is a reference to the term "manufacture" and I hope the minister, with his battery of legal experts there, can provide me with a definition of "manufacture". On page 9 there is a paragraph reading:
The minister shall be the sole judge-
Personally, I do not like this particular phrase because, in my opinion, that does not give the minister the power to be the sole judge but gives one of his officials the power to be the sole judge, thereby contributing to what I call bureaucratic dictatorship. I hope the minister will eliminate that phrase altogether.

I have a question to put to the minister that is occasioned by some correspondence. If a company in Canada purchased some plant machinery in the United States before budget time and delivery has not taken place as yet, what is the position with regard to this tax? Does the minister's statement of July 8 have any effect or is the deciding factor the old standard test of in transit, the signing of the original agreement or actual delivery? I may say that I bring this matter forward because I think there is a principle involved if the budget had a retroactive effect. This type of machinery might have been purchased ahead of time end it would be an uneconomic proposition for the company were the tax imposed on it afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax would not apply if the item in question had been cleared through customs at the date of the budget; otherwise, it would.

I just want to say, Mr. Chairman, that this brings out the hardship to which I referred. Here is a company which, with good intentions, purchased a piece of machinery in the United States. Naturally, the company would take into account the fact that it would cost so much to deliver the machinery. However, delivery was impossible, for justifiable reasons, and now the company is caught by this provision of the budget which has a retroactive effect. I would think some consideration should be given to this anomalous situation. It is not as if the company was aware that the sales tax or excise tax would be imposed. This would have been a consideration for them.
I am quite prepared to give this problem to the minister if this makes it easier. Perhaps he might have had correspondence with this company, but I did want to point out the unfairness of the retroactive feature of the budget and the effect that has on those who, with good intentions, have ordered machinery which could not be delivered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid that whenever there is a change in a tax of this kind or

whenever there is a change in the tariff, and there have been some recently, those changes come into effect immediately. It would be very difficult, I think, depending on the circumstances, to handle it differently. However, I am glad the hon. member brought this to my attention and if, in other cases, anything can be done about it in the future, I shall be glad to consider it. The precedents of the past have usually been that when a tax or tariff change is made, they apply from that date forward.

I should like to say a word or two about the proposal to tax rebuilt items, particularly rebuilt engines. In dealing with this proposal, I believe the minister said it was put forward because this type of remanufacturing, as I believe he called it, created unfair competition for the manufacturers of new items. I believe that is a debatable proposition. However, even if that view is accepted, there are two other principles in regard to this matter which I think are of importance.
In the first place, I should like to refer to the engine rebuilding plants which exist in western Canada, that part of the country with which I am familiar. Perhaps the situation is a little different in Ontario where you are closer to the factory that builds new engines. These rebuilding plants perform a very important service for farmers, contractors and country elevator people who use these engines. They are small industries which need to be encouraged.
The other point is that, as I say, these are all comparatively small industries and to apply a tax to them really amounts to discrimination in favour of the large engine manufacturers. I believe this policy will also create a large number of anomalies and I would hope, therefore, the minister and the government would give further consideration to the matter, particularly to the withdrawal of this tax in so far as rebuilt items are concerned, at least the rebuilt engines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 6 carry?
I am sorry, but I cannot allow this clause to be carried unless I receive an explanation from the minister with regard to the term "boxes for farm wagons".
I thought it was boxes for sardines.

I think the hon. member across the way should be recognized, Mr. Chairman. I do not know what his constituency is.

Excise Tax Act
With regard to these boxes for farm wagons, we in the west, as I said before six o'clock, do not use wagons any more on our farms. We use trucks. This term "wagon" is not defined by the Department of National Revenue in the same way as it is defined in the Canada Grain Act, namely as any vehicle which will take grain from a farm to an elevator. As a result, the farmers of western Canada are having to pay between $300 and $400 in tax on these articles for lack of a suitable definition. As I said earlier, one of my constituents spent more than $500 trying to get an explanation of this term "wagon". We cannot understand why the Department of National Revenue would not accept the term as defined by the Department of Finance. We have been told by officials of the Department of Finance that "wagon" does mean "truck"; but the Department of National Revenue would not accept that. They would not accept * that a box for a wagon or a box for a truck are exactly the same thing and are intended for the same purpose. In the light of the cost-price squeeze problem which we are facing in western Canada I cannot accept this clause as it is set down here, unless an explanation is forthcoming from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it is fair to say that the hon. member has explained his case very clearly, but the fact is that this reference to wagons has been in the act for a long time and is not being changed by this amending bill. It is not proposed to change it. There is no suggestion of changing it here. It is not proposed by the government to make a change in this particular item. A farm truck is a wagon and although wagons are exempt we must draw the line at making trucks exempt. A farm wagon is dedicated to use on the farm. A truck, on the other hand, is used for many other purposes besides agriculture. I am sorry that the government is not prepared to accept the hon. member's suggestion that this particular item be extended.
He also asked me before the adjournment why soft drinks are not being made exempt. All I can say in reply is that soft drinks have been subject to the tax for some time. To exempt them would cost the treasury about $12 million and in my opinion the treasury is not in a position to suffer a loss of revenue to that extent.

I do not think the minister got my point. I have no quarrel with him when he says that trucks should not be exempt. I am talking about the boxes that go on the truck or on the wagon. It is a grain box, and whether it is on a wagon or a truck should not make any difference. I should like

to get that point across to the minister. I am not saying that trucks should be exempt.
I have had the same argument with the department before. They have maintained time and time again that the box is part of the truck. To me the box is not part of the truck. It is not manufactured by the people who manufacture trucks. When a farmer goes to buy a truck with a grain box on it he has to make two separate purchases. The box is not made by the same people who make the chassis of the truck. He has to buy it from an implement dealer, and then we get into the argument about what an implement is.
I have a great deal of correspondence before me in connection with the argument I have had with the department before. I am not talking about a truck. I am talking about the box that goes on the truck or the box that goes on the wagon. The minister has said that this provision has been in the act for a long time. I realize that; but the point is that since it was originally put in the act progress has been made in farming. We do not use horses any more. If it is a wagon it is drawn by a horse. Now we have trucks that use the same type of box formerly used on a wagon. 1 see no difference in the bux at all, and all I am talking about is the box that goes on the truck.

Mr. Chairman, I think the point brought up by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek is an important one because these boxes found on trucks today are taking the place of boxes that used to be on wagons in years gone by. The minister said that the legislation has not been changed over a long period of years. Surely during such a long period of time there must be progress somewhere along the line. We are not going to sit back and take everything that was brought forward over the last 60 years and continue it simply because it has been in effect for a long period of time. That is a weak argument. A change has been suggested by the hon. member-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the greatest respect, the hon. member had six years in which he could have done something about it. I am perfectly prepared to consider this point very carefully but not at this moment.

The tone in which the Minister of Finance speaks would indicate that he is not prepared to take a few extra minutes to deal with the problem presented by these members. It is a good case and the minister should take a few extra minutes to consider it. I assure the minister that if he had taken a few extra minutes on some of these other items he would have had a lot less trouble.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am perfectly prepared to do that, but before making a change of this kind I would really like to know not only all the arguments in favour of the proposition but what arguments, if any, there may be against it.
Then is the minister willing to stand this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I recognize the difficulty here. As the hon. member said a few minutes ago, he is not arguing that the truck should not be taxed but he is arguing that the box that goes on the truck should be free of tax. So you have a beasty or you have an article, the basic part of which should not be free of tax, but it is argued that a piece of it should be free of tax. It seems to me, with all due respect to the hon. member, that this drives us into a rather difficult position, and it is for that reason that perhaps I have been less enthusiastic about accepting his proposition than I might otherwise have been.

Mr. Chairman, if the box was imported and there was an end user's certificate that it would only be used for agricultural purposes I think that would solve the problem. To me it does not make any difference if the box goes on a wagon or a truck, but apparently the minister is prepared to say that if it goes on a wagon it is exempt but if the same box goes on a truck it is taxable, which does not seem reasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because the wagon is exempt and the truck is not. I can see the hon. member's point of view, but I presume he can also see the point of view I am trying to present, that we are dealing with a wagon that is exempt and a truck which is not. The hon. member has suggested that if the box goes on a wagon it is exempt and therefore if it goes on a truck it should also be exempt. I am putting the point of view that the complete article, wagon and box, is exempt. The hon. member has pointed out that it is obsolete in the west but it still may be used occasionally in some other parts of Canada that are perhaps less progressive. But if we get into a situation where we are dealing with a hybrid, the main part of which is subject to tax and part of which is not, I am sure that in the end we will end up with a worse situation than if I had not accepted the proposal.

Let me try to clarify this point. I have contended in the past that the box is neither part of the wagon nor is it part of the truck, and so that I do not go off on a tangent I should like to read a few paragraphs of a letter I wrote to the department trying
Excise Tax Act
to put across my argument. They contend that the box is taxable under tariff item 438f. In my letter I said:
Item 438f deals with parts of motor vehicles.
A box is not a part of a motor vehicle.
I contend that a steel truck, grain or livestock box is not part of what is considered a motor vehicle or the chassis thereof, but rather an article to be mounted or attached thereto. Item 438a states such articles shall be valued separately and duty assessed under tariff items regularly applicable thereto.
In western Canada-
As I said before.
-and the same may be said of eastern Canada,-
I am not too sure about that.
-automotive dealers very seldom sell a farm truck or vehicle with steel grain box attached. If the farmer requires a grain box the normal procedure is for the farmer or dealer to obtain one from an implement dealer. Grain and livestock truck boxes are usually manufactured by those specialized in manufacturing agricultural implements and not from automotive manufacturers. Most automotive dealers price sheets list chassis only and do not include a price for a grain or livestock box.
Therefore, I contend a grain box should not be considered as a part of the truck, or vehicle, but considered under some other heading.
I do not care under which heading we consider it.
I further contend a steel grain or stock truck box could be included under the heading of agriculture implements-
This is already in the tariff item.
-for the following reason. In legal dictionaries, the term implement is defined as a thing of necessary use in any trade.
Certainly, a truck box is used in the trade of agriculture.
The word necessary is defined as those things to the doing of a thing which are reasonably required.
A box is essential to the truck if it is going to be used to haul grain. You can put the same box on a wagon or a truck with certain modifications. I do not see why you differentiate between the two.

I should like to add a few words to what has already been said by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. You can take the same box and put it on a truck, a wagon or a sleigh for that matter. Surely, the minister himself can see that this is the type of unit that can be used for agricultural purposes. The minister is saying that this is a complicated procedure through which we have to go before we can get an exemption. I recall, for example, that during the war the procedure was very simple. Eaton's and Simpson's had a blank form in their mail order catalogue and all you had to do was fill out the form to indicate that you were a farmer and that the particular item

Excise Tax Act
you were buying was for farm purposes. This was all that was required during the time of war. This method was devised by people who were getting a dollar a year. Now, however, we find this is an extremely complicated problem and the matter cannot be looked at for another year. This does not make sense.
This is an item that is being used on a farm. A man can take that same box off a truck and put it on a wagon or put it on a sleigh and use it for the same purpose. The only difference is that he uses a different method of propulsion. It seems to me that it would only take a few minutes for the minister to say that if a form were filled out signifying the equipment was for agricultural purposes, it would be exempt.

A few minutes ago the minister mentioned that a box for a wagon was exempt. So far as we are concerned in the west, when we think of a wagon we naturally think of the old steel wheeled wagon and that has been out of existence for a long time. The truck has now replaced it. However, if you wanted to get a truck the same size as the old wagon you could still buy this same wagon box for the now extinct wagon, put it on the truck and you would be home free. However, as a result of the fact that trucks today have a larger capacity you have to have a box of a larger size.
These boxes are for farm use almost entirely, I would say, and usually of wooden construction. The steel box is the only box that might have a dual purpose. I think it is just a matter of realizing that the wagon has almost disappeared as an implement for hauling grain. It is still used for small jobs around the farm, but for the purpose of hauling grain off the farm and into the elevator it is no longer used.

I think this is a good place for me to intervene since I have practised law as well as done a little bit of farming. It seems to me that the government should give consideration to the changing conditions as the result of rail line abandonment. The original purpose of a farm wagon was to draw grain a distance of seven miles which, under the Railway Act, was the shortest distance between two elevators. Obviously the grain is going to have to be drawn anywhere from 30 miles to 40 miles if this rail line abandonment legislation proceeds.
I draw to the minister's attention the phrase which has been referred to by my hon. friend, that this is a box for a farm wagon. This indicates the boxes are individual items. Perhaps the minister would agree to simply adding after the words "farm wagons", the

words "farm trucks". He would then have an amendment which would be quite plain. These would be separate items used either for farm wagons or farm trucks. I do not believe there would be any great difficulty about agreeing to that simple amendment which would meet the very reasonable request made by the hon. member.

A minute ago the minister mentioned the last six years. I do not know whether or not that was an invitation to discuss some of the events that took place during that period. We on this side of the house would be very glad to make reference to some of the things that are done in this particular bill. Reference has been made by the hon. member for Peace River to rail line transportation which bears directly on the changed situation in connection with agriculture in western Canada as it affects this particular item. For that reason, we would like the minister to give some recognition to this problem, at least more recognition than he has indicated in his remarks this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think all I can say is that I do not believe this is the time to make representations on this matter. If hon. members will make representations to me, I will go into them very carefully but I do not believe we can do it tonight.
We will make representations if the minister will give us an opportunity two months later to have another budget.

This is not the first time we have approached the department on this issue. I believe the hon. member for Peace River has brought up a very important point because in some parts of Saskatchewan some of these rail lines have been abandoned, necessitating the haulage of grain in bigger quantities longer distances. I say this is the place
