I would point out that it is customary, when a new tax is imposed on commodities, to apply it to goods sold after a certain date. The general rule for federal sales and excise tax changes is to have the new tax apply with respect to sales made, or goods cleared through customs, after midnight of the day on which the budget speech is delivered. In this way all persons are treated alike.
In the case of this year's tax changes, the sales tax on building materials and production machinery is intended to apply on and after June 14. In accordance with the usual rule it was not intended that the fact that goods had been ordered or prices quoted before June 14 would affect the imposition of the tax on goods sold after budget date.
It was recognized, however, that some manufacturers and some contractors would be caught in a very difficult position because of the imposition of the tax on all sales after June 13. If a manufacturer who was required to pay tax on goods sold by him after budget date was also required to sell those goods under the terms of an enforceable contract at a price which did not include the tax he might suffer a severe loss.
Similarly, a building contractor who was required to construct a building at a fixed price under an enforceable contract would find the price of his materials increased by the amount of the sales tax and because of this squeeze might be placed in a difficult financial position.
The government recognized these facts and the budget speech promised relief for those who were bound by fixed price contracts entered into on or before budget date. It should be noted that the purpose of this relief was not primarily to protect the eventual purchaser of goods. If the purchaser has a fixed price contract he is already protected. The purpose was to help the person caught between the tax and a commitment to supply goods at a price which did not permit addition of the tax.
In determining under what kinds of fixed price contract relief should be granted, consideration had to be given to the difficulties of ascertaining what were legally binding situations from which the vendor or contractor could not escape without having to absorb the tax himself or suffer some pecuniary penalty.
It became evident that bona fide contracts in writing signed by both parties prior to the budget date were capable of being both ascertained and verified. The same could be said of tenders made in writing prior to June

13 whereby the person submitting the tender was bound to enter into a contract and in default of doing so, would incur a pecuniary penalty, whether by forfeiture of a security deposit or otherwise.
It was realized when the line was drawn to include only these two types of formal contractual obligations that there would be a number of closely related or borderline cases where the commitments lacked the contractual characteristics of those just mentioned. For example, the government has been urged to accept as grounds for relief contracts which have arisen out of offers, or tenders made orally, and contracts which have arisen out of tenders not binding in the sense that the person making the tender would suffer a pecuniary loss if he did not proceed to sign a contract. It has also been asked to grant relief in respect of contracts with a guaranteed upset or maximum price, cost plus contracts and contracts related to leased property. All these requests have been examined carefully but it has been concluded that it would be unfair and unmanageable to base tax relief on any contracts other than those concluded in writing before June 14 or those concluded after that date in accordance witn the terms of a tender in writing which committed the person who submitted the tender to a pecuniary penalty if he failed to stand by his bid. Such contracts may include certain upset or maximum price contracts that have the elements of a fixed price contract, but would not include cost plus or percentage fee contracts.
To go beyond what I have indicated would open the door to claims in respect of a wide range of transactions where the manufacturer, contractor or supplier is not prevented from passing on the tax to the purchaser or user of the goods in question.
Although it is realized that this may not be an entirely satisfactory solution, particularly for those firms who conduct their affairs in a more informal manner and do not always put commitments down in a written con-tractural form, it must also be accepted by those who have given this matter careful thought that it would be administratively impossible to do other than rely on independent documentary evidence.

On second reading of the bill I said that we felt the bill was a combination of a piece of legislation which is already on the books and the proposed bill that the government introduced last year in connection with the establishment of a board. What I said at the time was that the only difference between the two pieces of legislation which the Conservative government had brought forward and this piece of legislation was in the objects of the bill, mostly as set out in clauses 9 and

Economic Council of Canada 10. I said then that our great fear was, in view of what the minister had said as to the theoretical approach that might be taken to this legislation, that the ideas of planning might be more compulsive than necessary, and that we should like to have some assurance from the minister that, while the bill was very broad in its terms, caution would be observed in proceeding with it. I said at the time that what we feared most was a proliferation of government forms to be filled out by both small and private business; more and more interference with private business, especially small businesses.
Before proceeding further, perhaps the minister at this point would give us some assurance that so far as possible the bill will not be an excuse for an advanced series of planning measures requiring the co-operation of business in making more returns and more investigations into their business; in suggesting things that they ought to do without the consent of such businesses. I should like to place this before the minister now. We feel that planning has its place, and a very important place, in the business world; but we also feel that at this time, when business is making an effort to recover and to produce more and obtain access io export markets we should not unduly burden it with nonproductive work or the proliferation of office work. I feel that to a large extent business wants to be left alone, and that the planning involved in this measure should proceed with as little interference with production as possible.
These are the points I asked the minister to clarify for us. I might say that some of us on this side of the house feel that the minister perhaps moves a little too fast, or is moving a little too fast, in his ideas, and that he may he more theoretical in his approach than practical-ana i do not say that unkindly. But our tear is that he may bring into this bill a series of planning measures that will not be useful at this particular time in our economic progress. If the minister would like to comment on this matter I would appreciate it.

And, with regard to this matter, I wonder if the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) recall certain words of the minister. I apologize, Mr. Chairman, for a slight impingement on the rules by quoting certain words which the minister used when discussing the motion for second reading. According to page 2087 of Hansard, he said:
To overcome our present difficulties, we need new policies, applied in a new spirit and within new administrative structures. In other words, we need a plan so that the various aspects of the economic policy will be well co-ordinated and so that the private sector can work in the same direction as the government towards the common objective of harmonious growth.
Mr. Chairman, I think that those fine words aim at full planning, and that this is only an effort on the part of the minister to tell us that the aim and philosophy of the economic council are complete planning in the public or private sectors.
I believe no one could infer anything else from these remarks.

I was also referring to certain statements made by the minister the other day. There was some indication he felt the private sector of the economy had been deficient. We wonder how he felt we might be able to cure these so-called economic ills which, he says, came about because of stagnation in the private sector. Is there to be an artificial stimulation of the private sector or is it through the stimulation of the public sector

that we hope to bring about a reinvigoration of the economy? Is it perhaps, by a combination of both? I think the answers to these points would be most constructive and it is most important we should get some clarification with regard to this. In the light of some of the philosophy which has permeated the Liberal party in the last couple of years and which has been evident in the speeches of Liberal party spokesmen old and new, but chiefly new, it seems we are entering upon an era of the planned economy. This is something I want to know: are we to have planning and, if we are to have planning, how is the government to guarantee the efficacy of the planning unless there is an effective degree of control? I am sure all hon. members will agree that controls breed controls, and if there is anything which is debilitating to the economy it is control and supercontrol. These are matters in which both businessmen and private individuals are deeply concerned. They are concerned at the direction which policies have tended to take and they have been interested in certain legislation which has been proposed, including provision for an economic council. I think we could perhaps have some light thrown by the minister on the future of this council.

While it is true that we in the opposition may have reservations about certain particulars in this bill, while we may feel there are provisions contained in it which are not sufficiently precise and which do not indicate how far the government is prepared to go in implementing the recommendations of the economic council, I think we are nevertheless encouraged by the fact that the government is prepared to create an economic council for Canada.
If the policies of the last two months to which we have been exposed in this house are any indication of the government's ability to govern this country in the absence of advice, then we look forward to the creation of a council which may provide hon. gentlemen opposite with an opportunity to accept advice enabling them to avoid some of the errors of the past ten weeks or so. We have in the course of this very evening considered certain government policies whose implementation can only have the effect of diminishing growth and retarding progress. In this bill, on the other hand, we find that if this economic council is created as outlined it will be entrusted with responsibility for advising, recommending, studying, exploring, encouraging, fostering, promoting and so on. All these tasks are being given to the council to do so as to encourage the government to find out what its responsibility is to the people of
Economic Council of Canada Canada and to the growth of the Canadian economy. On the face of the performance of the government since this session began this is essential because when one considers that as a consequence of policies so far announced it is conceivable that major developments in the province of British Columbia and, by projection, in other provinces throughout Canada could be retarded, it becomes clear that this government requires the assistance of recommendations, inquiries and so on by qualified people.
We do not know, of course, at this moment who the government intends to appoint to provide this assistance and advice. In order to know how effective this economic council may be, we shall have to be given some idea of the people who are to provide this advice to the government, and what their qualifications are. At the moment it is probably incumbent on us to be reasonably hopeful-to be encouraged by the fact that the government has taken up an idea from the former administration and is prepared to create a council to advise, to encourage, to promote and to study. We shall not argue with these objectives. At the same time we might ask: will the government pay any attention to this advice? On the basis of what we have seen so far, is it to be expected that this council will have any effect on policy? Will it, in fact, be able to persuade the government, on the basis of its studies, that there is a necessity in Canada for a fresh approach to the problems which confront us?
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka spoke of the undesirability of imposing on businessmen small or large the necessity of filling out more forms and questionnaires most of which do not seem destined to serve any practical purpose. Most hon. members are aware from their own experience or from the experience of others that in relation to one branch of government alone, the dominion bureau of statistics, a great many merchants and businessmen of one kind or another are required to devote a substantial part of the annual cost of their operations to filling out forms to provide information which apparently it never used or, even after it is assembled for use, is not comprehended. There are a great many businessmen in this country who are sympathetic to the idea of the government acquiring information on which to base policy, which would make it possible for them to thrive and prosper. But when they find that a substantial part of their time is devoted to doing the bookkeeping for the government, resulting in the services

Economic Council of Canada of many of their staff being effectively removed, they tend to question the efficacy of the type of legislation we have before us at this moment.
The idea of an economic council drawing upon the best advice that business and the professions in every phase of our economy can provide is a sound idea, but I think we also need some assurance that if we do draw on this experience, if we do draw upon the competence of qualified men from every segment of the Canadian economy, when they make recommendations they will be heeded, for if they are not this is an exercise in futility. I do not wish to unduly emphasize this, but if we go back to the business that has been under discussion in the house earlier tonight and the business that has been done in the house over the past two months we must realize that the present government has taken advice from no one who understood what policies are essential to the development of the economy of Canada. If they had taken such advice they would surely never have introduced some of the policies, either budgetary or legislative, that have been brought into the house in the last two

Mr. Chairman, I think that our first task is to restore our own confidence in our country and to decide what part we want to play in this rapidly changing world. Our country still possesses the same tremendous resources and the same people, while offering even greater possibilities than ten years ago, when its reputation was at its best, when we looked at the future with confidence and when the whole world considered us as the country which offered the best hopes and promises.
It is worth while trying to find out why confidence in Canada has declined. The main reason of the present lack of confidence in our country is the fact that we have failed to choose a formal and clear policy in the field of trade. The reason for this concern is of course that Canadians, as most other people, take an intelligent interest in their own financial affairs.
It may be that the reason for this lack of a well-defined economic policy lies in the fact that such a policy requires nowadays

trade in a rapidly changing world and that those alternatives require necessarily that decisions be taken which might cause discomfort in some fields, in some industries and would inevitably require that sacrifices be made in the interest of the general economy. Many disappointments face the ambitious persons who are not ready to make sacrifices. The true freedom is to make a choice and not simply to have a choice to make.
Mr. Chairman, we can no longer be satisfied with making mere distinctions between primary and secondary industry or between domestic and export industries. They are all interdependent. In most cases, the same company manufactures products to sell in Canada or outside and could not, therefore, without undergoing grave strains argue some day in favour of a freer trade for export products and try the next day to obtain more protection for its Canadian markets. Our industry provides a good example of that situation.
We have an important part to play in our economy. Should we fail to play that part, to take position on the important questions of today, in that case, if things went worse, we should have no one to blame but ourselves if, later on, the decisions made were not to our liking; and even if everything worked out for the best, our national effort

would be weakened by the indecision and the silence of the businessmen. It is imperative that there be some communication between the public and the private sectors but the voice of business on important questions has too often been confused and weak.
Mr. Chairman, the minister said that he wanted a planned economy. The word "planning" nowadays has a strong emotional connotation. It is being used indiscriminately and brings about violent reactions, which are either favourable or unfavourable.
The concept of national economic planning seems to have gained much more with us. But we are still very evasive when it comes to giving an exact definition of what we really mean by economic planning.
Is there one successful company without planning? We must reckon with the human element and individual freedom to decide what should be done to serve a company's best interests. The second prerequisite is to define a company's objectives. A man gives his best when he has been assigned definite objectives, knowing that he is free to attain them on his own initiative.
Both conditions are important. If you set objectives and limit the freedom of the individual trying to attain them, in general, he will never succeed. On the other hand, if he is given full freedom of action without any definite objectives, you will have confusion.
Both conditions are also necessary on a national scale. The objectives must be well defined. In other words, we have to do some planning; all sectors of our economy, that is, industry, labour, agriculture, etc., must be left free to experiment and choose with a view to attaining the national objectives. Such planning on a national scale is not synonymous with socialism and does not mean that the state must take over and control our economy. As a matter of fact, socialism, in its strictest meaning, carries the germ of its own defeat and not only on the theoretical level, because we think that it entails an inferior way of life, but on the level of practical achievement, since an economy where administration is too centralized and controlled will be less successful, produce less and will be less efficient than the one where the individual is left free to choose and make his own decisions.
But personal initiative has little chance to give the best results on a national scale unless objectives are clearly set out. And such national objectives can only be established when the government has clearly de-

fined and explained them and shown their benefits, after having consulted all economic groups.
We are today facing a serious problem of surplus capacity which, for several years, will cause serious difficulties in the marketing field. During those years, we should be able to rely on a national policy ensuring a freer and easier access to world market for our products, on a fiscal policy enabling us to maintain employment, to improve our equipment and productivity and, lastly on a transportation policy which will permit us to compete in Canada and abroad.
Finally, we must, because of the size of our industry, establish and publicize our objectives five to ten years ahead, so that the government, as well as industry and labour, can take the necessary steps to reach this goal.
Mr. Chairman, it is to be hoped that when the minister is talking of economic planning, these are the directives which he intends to give to the economic council. But I doubt that the economic council will reach its objectives, because the minister has not provided in the bill for the necessary financial reforms, in order to make the responsibilities of the Bank of Canada more flexible, to increase the purchasing power, in brief to achieve the production level which would make financially possible what is physically desirable in Canada.
